<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is the Java-based core engine for SuperTokens – an open‐source authentication provider that powers secure login and session management. In addition to the core authentication “recipes” (such as email/password, social login, passwordless, multi-factor authentication, multi-tenancy, etc.), the repository also contains components for command‐line interface (cli), a downloader module (to fetch or manage updates/dependencies), and an enterprise edition (the “ee” folder) which extends core features. The README further outlines that SuperTokens integrates with Frontend and Backend SDKs, and the core handles the HTTP service and underlying database operations.

Below is how you should reason about and structure your system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Core Authentication Engine: Represented by the main “src” directory (including packages such as authRecipe, emailpassword, emailverification, session, jwt, webserver, etc.). This component implements the core HTTP API endpoints for sign-in, sign-up, token management, and various authentication flows.
   • Enterprise Modules: The “ee” directory contains the enterprise-specific features (e.g., extended licensing, feature flag checks, cronjobs for license validity, etc.). This can be drawn as an extension to the core authentication engine.
   • CLI Module: The “cli” directory wraps a command-line interface for administrative tasks (installation, starting/stopping processes, printing help, and version management). It communicates with the core engine (possibly to trigger build processes or administrative commands).
   • Downloader Module: The “downloader” directory contains code to help fetch or update necessary parts (likely interacting with remote repositories or updating jars). This module can be considered as a support or integration component.
   • Build & CI/CD: Directories like “.circleci” and “.github” (with workflows and Dockerfiles) highlight the CI/CD and automated testing/integration pipelines. Although not part of runtime architecture, they are essential for deployments.
   • External Integrations: Via the storage layer, session management, database connectors, and webserver APIs, the core interacts with user databases and external client SDKs (frontend and backend). Represent these as external sources in your diagram.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   • External SDKs (Frontend & Backend) call the SuperTokens Core’s API endpoints (hosted on an embedded webserver).
   • The Core communicates with its Storage Layer (both in-memory and/or on-disk databases) to manage user data, sessions, and tokens.
   • Within the core, distinct “recipes” (emailpassword, passwordless, multi-tenancy, etc.) encapsulate specific authentication/logging logic. They interact with a central configuration system and share utilities (logging, rate limiter, JWT handling, etc.).
   • The CLI module acts as a user-facing tool that internally calls the core services or sets up configuration.
   • The Downloader module might be used during installation and upgrade processes, fetching jars/build artifacts.
   • The Enterprise edition (“ee” module) provides enhancements that integrate and extend the core functionalities. A dependency arrow may illustrate that “ee” augments the core system.
   • CI/CD pipelines (denoted by .circleci and .github directories) are used to build, test, and package the application for deployment (e.g. via Docker or as a jar).

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns & Technical Choices:
   • Modular/Layered Architecture: The project breaks down into distinct modules (core, cli, downloader, ee) with specialized responsibilities.
   • Plugin/Extensibility Pattern: The use of “authRecipe” modules and other feature-specific packages suggests a plugin-like mechanism where new authentication recipes can be added.
   • RESTful API & HTTP Microservice: The “webserver” package indicates that the core exposes HTTP APIs. Use directional arrows for API calls from external clients to the core.
   • Use of Gradle Build Scripts: Gradle (build.gradle, settings.gradle) configures the project compilation and packaging. Although not directly part of the runtime diagram, these indicate a build pipeline that can be annotated.

4. Include Relevant Technologies & Frameworks:
   • Java: The entire project is implemented in Java.
   • Embedded HTTP Server: Likely using embedded Tomcat or similar lightweight server (as inferred from “webserver” package).
   • Docker: The presence of Dockerfiles in CI directories and for distribution.
   • Gradle: For building and dependency management.
   • CI/CD scripts: GitHub and CircleCI workflows for continuous integration.

5. Tailor Your Diagram to the Specific Project Type:
   • Since this is a backend core service (that supports full stack applications via external SDKs), ensure that you clearly separate the authentication APIs (core engine) from external client interactions.
   • Emphasize modularity by splitting the diagram into as many logical components as possible, e.g. the core engine, enterprise enhancements, CLI tool, downloader support, storage layer, and external API consumers.

6. Guidelines for Diagram Drawing:
   • Use clear labels for each component: For example, “SuperTokens Core (Authentication Engine)”, “Enterprise Extensions (EE)”, “CLI Module”, “Downloader Module”, “Webserver & API Endpoints”, “Storage Layer”, etc.
   • Represent data flow with directional arrows: Illustrate how requests flow from front-end/backend SDKs to the core engine, how the CLI triggers administrative commands, and how the core interacts with the database or storage layer.
   • Use color coding or distinct shapes: For instance, use one color for runtime modules (core, ee, webserver), another for support modules (CLI, Downloader), and yet another for infrastructure elements (CI/CD pipelines, build scripts, external integrations).
   • Include annotations to outline which modules represent authentication “recipes” (passwordless, emailpassword, OAuth, etc.) and also how they communicate with shared utilities, like logging and configuration.

By following these steps and emphasizing detail in each key component and their interactions, you’ll produce a comprehensive and accurate system design diagram for the SuperTokens core project. This diagram should capture the high-level architecture while breaking down internal modularity and external communications, aligning closely with both the file structure provided and the README’s description of the system’s purpose and architecture.
</explanation>
